snippet.title: Engineer Hess and the Johnstown Flood
snippet.description:
Watch The Great Johnstown Flood here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q_B3MaLgXUo

A work train is stopped while its crew inspects a landslide that wiped out the tracks when a 75 foot wall of water came crashing down the valley towards them. The dam up river has collapsed and a torrential flood is surging downstream.

Engineer Hess throws the train into reverse and races the floodwater, closing in on him. He tied a rope around the steam whistle so it blasted one long, continuous cry as he approached the nearby town. This caught the attention of the conductor of another train sitting idle nearby, who shouted for his passengers to abandon the train and run for higher ground. They ran, but few would escape the terrible flood closing in on them.

Engineer Hess kept his train going with the whistle blasting until he passed the spot closest to his house, when he leapt from the locomotive and ran for his family, narrowly escaping the destruction that swept away his train.

In 1863, a mysterious man with no legs washed ashore on a remote beach in Nova Scotia. He couldn’t speak, couldn’t explain who he was, and refused to tell his story. Locals called him Jerome — and for half a century, his silence became one of Canada’s greatest unsolved mysteries.

In this documentary, we travel to the sites where Jerome lived, uncover the real history behind the legend, and explore how one man’s isolation came to define a century of folklore along the Bay of Fundy. From the beach at Sandy Cove to the Acadian villages of Meteghan and Digby Neck, we retrace the story that inspired books, films, and myths around the world — and finally reveal the truth hidden beneath the mystery.

This film is based on original research, contemporary records, and the writings of historian Fraser Mooney Jr., whose work helped uncover Jerome’s likely origins.

snippet.title: Worst Public Road in America - The Lausanne Turnpike
snippet.description:
Explore the Ghost Town of Lausanne here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_u5MUuwynhw

This old turnpike in Pennsylvania was once called the worst public road in America, where travelers were frequently attacked by bandits. This was the Lausanne Turnpike, originally a Native American trade route, later widened for stagecoaches in the early 1800s. But as trains took over, the road was abandoned to outlaws. Travelers risked ambushes from bandits, and stagecoaches dragged logs behind them to avoid runaway crashes on steep hills. The once-bustling Landing Tavern became a ghost of its former self, finally abandoned in 1873. Now? The entire town of Lausanne is buried under rubble. Today, only the ruins—and the legends—remain.

Our team spent almost a week aboard the SS Milwaukee Clipper in Muskegon, Michigan, and that gave us the opportunity to conduct a lifeboat drill in the middle of the night. These lifeboat davits are similar to Titanic's, giving us an excellent, first hand understanding of how Titanic's lifeboat davits worked.

snippet.title: How a 1,000-Ton Historic Church Was Moved Across Salem
snippet.description:
The team faces brutal blizzards and ancient curses as they attempt a record-breaking move - relocating a colossal 200-year-old church in Salem, Massachusetts.

In this gripping episode of Monster Moves, witness the nerve-wracking journey to move Salem’s historic First Baptist Church nearly 60 meters down a steep hill. With courthouse expansion threatened by a legal backlog and the town’s storied past of witch trials looming large, a team of expert house movers must save the beloved landmark from demolition. The plan? Reinforce the fragile, 1,000-ton brick structure, navigate icy terrain, and align 280 wheels for a precise touchdown - all before winter’s worst hits.

Watch as Jerry Matico and his crew tackle engineering nightmares, from crumbling masonry and tight city streets to snowstorms that could halt progress for months. Discover how the team’s innovative use of steel beams, hydraulic jacks, and sheer determination transforms the abandoned church into a new law library, securing its place in Salem’s future. Along the way, you’ll get a front-row seat to construction mishaps, supernatural blessings from local witches, and the relentless drive required for record-breaking building moves.

snippet.description:
Fall Asleep To Real Maritime Mysteries: Titanic, Mary Celeste. Just 1 of many shipwrecks | Untraveled Mysteries

Before Titanic, there was another ship that turned the North Atlantic into hell.
In 1854, the SS Arctic—the pride of the White Star Line—collided in heavy fog and descended into chaos.
The crew stole every lifeboat, mothers were left to drown, and the captain watched his own 11-year-old son vanish beneath the waves.
It was the first great ocean disaster of the steam age—and the world tried to forget it.

But the sea never forgets.
From the cursed SS Arctic, to the vanishing Mary Celeste, to the shattered SS Laurel whose captain survived alone for fifty-four hours off the coast of Oregon—
these are the true maritime nightmares that history buried beneath the waves.

Dive with us through shipwrecks, betrayals, and forgotten logbooks—
because behind every calm sea lies a crime no one ever confessed to.

snippet.title: The Longest Anyone Has Ever Been Lost at Sea
snippet.description:
Maybe the most famous castaway case is Jose Salvador Alvarenga. he was documented to have been adrift at sea for 438 days. It's one of the most miraculous stories of survival in history, and its easy to see why. Beyond just the gruelling physical aspects, there’s something innately identifiable about the mental struggle of drifting endlessly in the open ocean. As incredible as his story is, though, and although it’s often cited as the longest time adrift at sea, there is another story, from two centuries earlier, that, if the records are accurate, is the true record for the longest time adrift. This is the horrifying and tragic story of the Tokujo Maru

snippet.title: Britain's Lost Treasures: Secrets of Stonehenge, King Arthur & Ancient Hoards Uncovered
snippet.description:
Discover the secrets of Britain’s ancient past - from Stonehenge mysteries to Dark Age palaces and lost Roman treasures - all revealed by groundbreaking archaeology.

Join Digging for Britain as we follow archaeologists on a thrilling journey across the West of Britain, capturing their most exciting discoveries of 2016. Witness firsthand as experts unearth everything from Neolithic double henges near Stonehenge and vast hoards of Iron Age coins in Jersey, to hidden World War I trenches on Salisbury Plain. Each dig is documented through “dig diaries,” offering you a front-row seat to moments of discovery that are rewriting British history.

In this episode, you’ll see the unearthing of Britain’s first doublehenge, shedding light on ancient rituals and ceremonies linked to Stonehenge. Travel to Jersey for the world’s largest Iron Age coin hoard, revealing the terror of the Roman invasion and the wealth of Celtic tribes. Explore Tintagel in Cornwall, where an incredible Dark Age palace challenges myths about Britain’s “dark ages” and hints at royal power and global trade connections. We’ll also visit mysterious burial sites in Hereford and South Wales, where unique funerary rituals and poignant infant burials reveal how past communities honored their dead and navigated times of upheaval.

Through expert lab analysis and privileged museum access, the episode delves into the meaning behind every artifact - from axes and pottery to coins, torques, and personal items left behind by soldiers. These finds offer an intimate glimpse into the lives, beliefs, and resilience of Britain’s ancestors, forever changing our understanding of the past.

snippet.title: Why Edmund Fitzgerald Sank, 13 Larger Ships Didn't? Great Lakes Largest Ships Curse | Fall Asleep To
snippet.description:
Why did the Edmund Fitzgerald sink while 13 larger ships survived? Uncover the dark secrets, conspiracies, and mysteries behind the Great Lakes' largest ships.

Why did the Edmund Fitzgerald sink in 1975, taking all 29 crew members with her? Why did the Carl D. Bradley break apart in 1958, killing 33 sailors? Yet somehow, 13 ships LARGER than both of them have survived for over 50 years without a single disaster?

This isn't just a documentary. This is a 4-hour deep dive into one of history's most chilling maritime mysteries.

🔍 WHAT YOU'LL DISCOVER
- Why the Carl D. Bradley, at 639 feet, sank after 31 years of perfect service
- The 5 competing theories behind the Edmund Fitzgerald's mysterious disappearance
- How 33 men died in 1958 while only 2 survived 16 hours in freezing water
- The "November Curse" — why most Great Lakes disasters happen in this one month
- Why 13 ships over 1,000 feet long have NEVER had a fatal accident in 50+ years
- The engineering secrets that make modern ships unsinkable... or do they?
- Cover-ups, unreported incidents, and the evidence that was hidden
- Why no ship longer than 1,013 feet has been built in 44 years (conspiracy?)

⚓ THE TRAGEDIES EXPLAINED
CARL D. BRADLEY (1958)
- 639 feet long, broke in half during a November storm
- 33 of 35 crew members died in Lake Michigan
- Unreported structural damage covered up by the company
- The longest-reigning "Queen of the Lakes" for 22 years
- Why did the Coast Guard and the company have conflicting stories?

EDMUND FITZGERALD (1975)
- 729 feet long, vanished in minutes on Lake Superior
- All 29 crew members lost, no distress call sent
- Made famous by Gordon Lightfoot's haunting song
- 5 theories: Hatch failure? Shoal strike? Rogue waves? Structural failure? All of the above?
- Why is the wreck site protected by a $1 million fine in Canada?

DANIEL J. MORRELL (1966)
- 603 feet long, split in half in Lake Huron
- 28 of 29 crew died in one of the coldest nights on record
- The sole survivor's impossible story of survival
- A tragedy overshadowed by Fitzgerald but equally horrifying

WHITE HURRICANE (1913)
- The deadliest storm in Great Lakes history
- 12 ships sunk in 3 days, 254 lives lost
- Waves over 35 feet, hurricane-force winds
- Changed maritime safety forever

🌊 THE NOVEMBER CURSE
- November 11, 1913: 18 ships sunk
- November 18, 1958: Carl D. Bradley
- November 29, 1966: Daniel J. Morrell
- November 10, 1975: Edmund Fitzgerald

snippet.title: America's *Other* Declaration of Independence & the Anti-Rent War | HISTORY This Week
snippet.description:
July 4, 1839. Sixty-three years after 1776—and centuries after the medieval period—feudalism is alive and well in the United States.

High on a rocky plain in upstate New York, a crowd of tenant farmers gathers in the village of Berne to read aloud a declaration of independence… but not the one you're thinking of. These families are still bound to a landlord by perpetual leases their grandfathers signed, owing bushels of wheat and a share of every sale for as long as the land exists. 

Today they're done. They call their leases "voluntary slavery" and vow to "take up the ball of the Revolution where our fathers stopped it." It's the opening shot of the Anti-Rent War,  a revolt that will pit disguised farmers against sheriffs and posses across the Hudson Valley, and force New York to ask whether a feudal bargain has any place in a republic. 

How did manor lords survive the Revolution? And what would it finally take to break their grip?

snippet.title: 3 Hours of Incredible Ship History
snippet.description:
In the throes of her sinking Titanic’s funnels come crashing down - but what about their engineering made it happen? In the wake of the second world war cargo and passenger ships mysteriously begin breaking in half - and its up to engineers to try to figure out why. Germany builds some of the greatest passenger liners or all time - but soon they are taken away. In the 1960s survivors of the Titanic disaster watch the movies and react to Hollywood’s early depictions of the tragedy. The magnificent SS Strathnaver heralds a new age for P&O line as they struggle in an increasingly competitive industry - and finally cameramen capture some of the most dramatic events as real ships sink on film. 

Oceanliner Designs explores the design, construction, engineering and operation of history’s greatest vessels– from Titanic to Queen Mary and from the Empress of Ireland to the Lusitania. Join maritime researcher and illustrator Michael Brady as he tells the stories behind some of history's most famous ocean liners and machines!

snippet.title: The History of Ceramics Podcast: George E. Ohr - The Mad Potter of Biloxi
snippet.description:
Paul Greenhalgh and Stephanie Rozene travel to the American South at the end the 19th C to explore the life and work of George E. Ohr - otherwise known as the Mad Potter of Biloxi. Overlooked for much of his life this eccentric character worked tirelessly creating innovative, wild and exquisitely crafted art pottery. He was a renowned showman using slogans, banners and sales gimmicks to market his wares and was the self proclaimed "world's best art-potter". His life’s work remained undiscovered gathering dust in a garage for decades before an antiques dealer happened upon them in his son's auto shop. Today his legacy is firmly recognised as a founding father of the art pottery movement and there is a museum in his name, designed by Frank Gehry, in his hometown of Biloxi.

snippet.title: Shepard Fairey: Why Protest Art Belongs Everywhere
snippet.description:
"There's a lot of debate about where protest art should live. My opinion is that it should live everywhere."

In this definitive monologue essay, legendary contemporary street artist and designer Shepard Fairey (the creative force behind OBEY Giant) traces his journey from a punk-rock-obsessed teenager to one of the most influential political artists of the 21st century.

From the viral, mischievous rise of his 1989 'Andre the Giant has a Posse' sticker to the global impact of the Barack Obama 'Hope' poster and the 'We the People' series, Fairey explores how art serves as an essential counter-argument to the dominant culture.

He delves deep into his early artistic influences—from the raw energy of the Reagan-Thatcher era and punk flyers to Barbara Kruger, Russian Constructivism, and Heidegger’s theory of phenomenology. Beyond the gallery walls, he reflects honestly on the physical dangers of his work, detailing his 18 arrests, police clashes, and his lifelong commitment to standing up and speaking out.

Discover the history, the mechanics, and the philosophy of an artist who believes that if something is worth saying, it's worth saying with style.

snippet.title: The Disturbing 1840 Southern Australian Expedition
snippet.description:
The Australian continent, much like Canada, despite its massive land mass, has only narrow pockets of habitability. If you look at a population map of the two countries, you can almost pinpoint exactly where those areas are. The areas with the best climates usually already have the largest populations. Obviously, though, much of Australia’s sparsely populated interior is harsh for the exact opposite reason that Canada’s is. Much of Australia is simply too hot and too dry to support large-scale settlement. Interestingly, in the 1800s, as new settlers made their way across the continent, they hoped that further inland would be similar to other continents. They hoped for lush forests, rivers, and fertile land. And the only way to truly figure out what was there was to make expeditions into the unknown. As we now know, in many regions those expectations proved disastrously wrong, and many of the expeditions would end horribly as a result. This is the Eyre Expedition, and as always, viewer discretion is advised.
